claims.overstatement: None material. The claim correctly calls the heat-loss mechanism an inference (heat production was not measured), keeps the low dose and cocaine-naive sample as study conditions, and reports the clubs/hot-weather idea as untested speculation. Wording points: (1) 'skin blood flow was 49 against 70 in 100 of its maximum' is forearm cutaneous vascular conductance (laser-Doppler flux divided by mean arterial pressure, as % of the site maximum), as the magnitude says; because end-of-heating pressure was higher with cocaine (92 against 87 mm Hg), flow itself would differ somewhat less than conductance, so 'skin vascular conductance' or 'skin blood flow relative to blood pressure' is more exact. (2) The Figure 1 end values read about 37.79 against 37.55 C at about 38 min (gap about 0.23 C on the figure's own bracket), so '37.8 against 37.5' slightly widens the gap; 'about 37.8 against 37.55' would match the figure.
claims.note: All text numbers in the statement and magnitude match pp. 787-788. Editors' calculation recomputed: difference 0.31 C with paired t on 6 df; P = 0.01 gives t = 3.707, SE 0.084, 95% CI 0.105 to 0.515; P = 0.002 gives t = 5.208, SE 0.060, 95% CI 0.164 to 0.456; same as the claim (with P rounding, the first interval could run from about 0.09-0.13 to 0.49-0.54). 'Number contributing at 37.86 C not stated' is fair: the paper calls it the highest common oesophageal temperature without a count, and Figure 1 shows the lidocaine mean only about 37.55 C at the end of the plotted time. Text-figure inconsistency the claim inherits but does not need to fix: at the same temperature Figure 2 (p. 789) reads about 54 against 67% of maximum and about 0.86 against 1.07 mg/cm2 per min, and its legend gives P < 0.01, while the text gives 49 +/- 9 against 70 +/- 5% (P = 0.03) and 0.8 +/- 0.2 against 1.0 +/- 0.1 (P = 0.04). Sex split of the 7 participants not given.

claims.overstatement: None for the Marzuk part: the claim keeps association language, states the unadjusted day comparison and the unknown exposures, and correctly treats the cocaine-specificity reading and the homicide/traffic argument as the authors' readings. Two small precision points: (1) the 10 heat deaths whose dates helped set the 31.1 C threshold come from 1990-1995, so they overlap the 1993-1995 test years (their hottest date, 39.4 C, equals the hottest days of the test period, July 1995); the split-sample test is therefore not wholly independent of the threshold choice, which the claim could say. (2) 'Deaths from opiates without cocaine' is the paper's group 2, which also admits cocaine or metabolite in clinically insignificant amounts.
claims.note: Every Marzuk number in the statement and magnitude matches the printed page. Editors' calculations recomputed (Poisson, log rate ratio): cocaine 341/146 against 1667/949 days, RR 1.330 (1.183 to 1.494); opiates 118/146 against 675/949, RR 1.136 (0.934 to 1.382); ratio of the two 1.170 (0.932 to 1.469); expected hot-day cocaine deaths at the other-day rate 256.5, excess 84.5 (4.2% of 2,008). All as stated. Sensitivity check with the printed daily SDs instead of Poisson variance (cocaine variance/mean 1.21 on hot days, 1.07 on other days): cocaine 1.17 to 1.51, opiates 0.93 to 1.39, ratio 0.92 to 1.49, so the 'somewhat too narrow' caveat is right and the conclusions do not change. Percentages recomputed: 136/719 = 18.9%, 766/3919 = 19.5%, 12/126 = 9.5%, 71/689 = 10.3%, 10/40 = 25%, 10/48 = 20.8%.

claims.overstatement: Slight, in one phrase: the paper says only rodents were used and that MOST of the animal studies gave the pre-treatments by injection (p. 174), not all; some gave antioxidants before and after MDMA. Smaller points: the paper glosses the comedown as the acute recovery period (p. 169), not 'the days after'; the paper reports no validation of its questionnaire rather than saying it was not validated; how often the listed strategies (Table 4) were used was not asked (p. 173), but how often people tested pills and preloaded or postloaded was asked (pp. 171-172). Understated: the magnitude lists the reasons 45.5%, 32.7% and 18.2% but leaves out the third most common, increasing the pleasurable effects of ecstasy, 21.8% of the 55 (Table 6), which shows that pre- and postloading were not only protective in intent (a finding about motives, to be stated without naming products or amounts if used).
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this source matches the printed text and tables (checked on the rendered pp. 169-174). Recomputed: ever tested 100 - 61.2 = 38.8% (45 of 116; summing the five categories gives 38.7% because of rounding), same as the editors' figure; preloaders 48 and postloaders 55 of 116; changed use 61 of 116 = 52.6%; the chi-squares reproduce from the printed percentages (preloading by more than 50 occasions 29/53 against 19/63, chi2 7.16; postloading 32/53 against 23/63, chi2 6.58; postloading by monthly use 33/59 against 20/55, chi2 4.38). 'About 30 tests': 10 listed variables x 3 outcomes (changed use, preloading, postloading) = 30, alpha 0.05 (0.025 when non-normal), no correction; gender differences were also tested and reported only if significant (p. 170), so 30 is a minimum. Editors' interval: +/-9 points is right for whole-sample shares (41.4% of 116: +/-9.0; 47.4%: +/-9.1), but shares among the 46 and 54 who listed products and the 55 who gave reasons carry about +/-12 to +/-14 points (5-HTP before 41.3% of 46, Wilson 28.3-55.7%; comedown 45.5% of 55, 33.0-58.5%). 'Harm-reduction websites': the paper says an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (p. 169); the acknowledgements name RaveSafe's e-newsletter and the Pill Reports website (p. 175), and RaveSafe is described as a harm reduction organisation (p. 169), so the wording is fair. Response rate: 98 questionnaires were handed out through acquaintances, the web route has no denominator and the split of the 116 by route is unknown (pp. 169, 175), so no response rate can be computed, as the claim says. No dosing or potentiation content in the claim; the 5-HTP and serotonin-syndrome lines report findings and the authors' caution only.

claims.overstatement: None material; the claim itself limits what the series can show (no rates, no comparison). Three wording points: (1) 'so most deaths were attributed from the circumstances' is an inference: the paper reports hydrocarbons found in 44 deaths without saying how many were autopsied or tested or how the other 66 were classed; 'for most deaths no toxicological confirmation is reported' is exact. (2) The author's uncertainty (p. 2079) is about what caused the terminal event with panic (arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, the excitement of light anaesthesia, a stress-hormone crisis, or a combination), not only about what caused the panic. (3) The author's proposed mechanism names raised carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) as an intensifier alongside stress and activity (abstract, p. 2075; p. 2079), which the claim's summary leaves out; and the low-toxicity judgement came from 'human and animal experiments' (p. 2075), not animal tests alone.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude was checked on the rendered pages. Editors' sums of the Figure 2 map legends reproduce exactly: aerosol fluorocarbon (with or without trichloroethane) 36 + 10 + 13 = 59; 1,1,1-trichloroethane 9 + 3 + 17 = 29; toluene 6 + 2 = 8; benzene 1 + 4 + 2 = 7; gasoline 3 + 1 = 4; toluene with trichloroethane 1 + 1 = 2; unidentified hydrocarbon 1; regions 57 + 18 + 35 = 110. 18/110 = 16.4%. Table rows sum to 18. No category in the key is an alkyl nitrite. The yearly panels of Figure 2 do not add up to the map totals (benzene about 6 against 7, trichloroethane about 26 against 29, fluorocarbon propellants about 58 against 59, with points not on whole numbers), and they combine 1968 with early 1969 (survey to 1 April 1969), so the 'sharp rise' is counts without denominators, as the claim says.

claims.overstatement: None material. 'Reduced' is causal, but the within-person randomized crossover with an objective outcome supports it for these conditions, and the claim states the limits (one small dose, young men only, no impairment measure, no printed meal-versus-fasting test, mechanism not measured, composition question underpowered). Two small precision points: (1) time to peak is counted from the start of alcohol dosing (Methods, p. 522), so 'peak came 30 to 90 minutes after drinking' should read 'after the start of drinking' (drinking took up to 15 min); (2) the protein-rich breakfast had 9.0 and 9.6 in 100 more energy than the carbohydrate- and fat-rich ones, i.e. about 9 to 10 in 100.
claims.note: Every number from this source checked on the rendered pages (abstract p. 521; Methods p. 522; Results p. 523; Table 1 p. 524). Editors' calculations recomputed and reproduced: meal peaks 43.2, 53.9 and 57.5 in 100 of the fasting peak (protein-, fat-, carbohydrate-rich); meal AUCs 39.6, 55.0 and 50.4 in 100 of the fasting AUC; protein-rich peak 19.9 and 24.9 in 100 lower than the fat- and carbohydrate-rich peaks, AUC 28.1 and 21.6 in 100 lower. With the five-condition residual SD (5.1 mg/dl; 465.2 mg/dl.min) and SE of a within-person difference = s_res x sqrt(2/9) (2.40 mg/dl; 219.3 mg/dl.min), the meal-fasting differences are 5.9, 5.4 and 7.3 SE for peaks and 6.6, 7.3 and 8.8 SE for AUCs: about 5 to 9, as stated (assumes sphericity). CVs recomputed from means and SDs match Table 1 except the intravenous AUC (446/4786 = 9.3%, printed 10%), which the claim does not use. Two qualifiers the claim could carry: (a) Figure 1f suggests the fed-versus-fasting difference in time to reach zero is under an hour (meal mean curves near zero at about 190-200 min; the fasting mean is about 6 mg/dl at its last plotted point, about 190 min, and only a dashed extension reaches zero at about 235 min), smaller than the authors' 1 to 2 h, which the claim already treats as not measured; (b) the authors attribute the slow fasting elimination rate (about 10 against an often-cited 15 mg/dl per hour) to the 10-12 h fast itself (p. 524), so the fasting comparator may itself have slowed elimination. The authors' unpublished observation that the food effect was larger the shorter the interval between meal and drink (p. 525) is not data from this study; the claim's 'did not test ... longer gaps' is correct.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the panic finding: 'increases' rests on the within-person, blinded placebo comparison (121 of 237 after caffeine, no panic attack after placebo in any study; 8 of 10 studies randomized the order), not on the pooled ratio, and the claim limits it to the doses, setting and medication-free state studied. Slight understatement on anxiety: the claim says only 2 studies reported placebo anxiety data, which matches the abstract and Results 3.5.1, 1st paragraph, but the same section also says 3 studies gave change data for both conditions and that all 5 studies that compared caffeine with placebo statistically found a larger anxiety rise after caffeine, the 4 of them with controls a larger rise in panic disorder (p. 26). The cups conversion is labelled as the authors' equivalence and reads as a description of study conditions, not advice.
claims.note: All numbers recomputed: 121/237 = 51.05%; 69/128 = 53.9%; 2/115 = 1.74%; risk difference 52.2 points; 52/109 = 47.7%; the Table 1 counts sum to these totals when Klein et al.'s group is 5 of 7 (printed 5/17). exp(3.47) = 32.1, exp(2.06) = 7.85, exp(4.87) = 130.3. From the Table 1 counts of the six two-group studies, a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratio without continuity correction is 32.03 (log 3.467) with a Greenland-Robins log-scale 95% CI of 2.06 to 4.87, which reproduces the text exactly; Fig. 4 prints 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) with chi-square(5) = 1.58 and I2 = 0% against the text's Q(5) = 8.45, so 'two incompatible pooled risk ratios' is right. Anxiety: from the Fig. 3 study values (SE from each 95% CI), DerSimonian-Laird with Hartung-Knapp intervals reproduces the printed 1.02 (0.08 to 1.96) and, without Nardi et al. 2009 (ref 38, g 2.51, the study the funnel plot flags), gives 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37), as the claim says; a plain z-interval would give 0.25 to 1.19, so the claim's interval follows the method the printed interval implies. Cups: 400/100 = 4 and 750/100 = 7.5. '8 of the 10 come from two research groups' is not stated by the review but follows from its reference list: Uhde is an author of refs 34, 51, 53 and 60 and Nardi first author of refs 38-41 (pp. 30-31); the other two are Charney 1985 and Masdrakis 2015, which also give the 1985-2015 range. One unresolved point: 'about 750 mg' is the review's conversion of Charney et al.'s 10 mg/kg at 75 kg (p. 25), but Table 1 describes that preparation as caffeine citrate (p. 25) and the review does not say whether 10 mg/kg refers to caffeine or to the salt (caffeine citrate is about half caffeine by weight). If it is the salt, that study gave about 375 mg of caffeine, which would change the 400 to 750 mg range and 'no study tested less than 400 mg'; only the primary paper can settle it.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The paper says only rodents were used and that MOST of the animal studies it mentions gave the pre-treatments by injection (p. 174, Discussion 13th paragraph), not all; some gave antioxidants before and after MDMA (11th paragraph). Read: 'the protective evidence comes only from rodent studies, most with injected pre-treatments'. The same wording appears in the card's interpretation_gap.claimed and in the claim. Locators are right (Discussion 11th to 14th paragraphs, pp. 174-175).

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary high: no frame, self-selected partly through harm-reduction channels, unknown response rate. Domain judgments agree, including 'partial yes' for items 3, 5, 6 and 8 with reasons (documented extension). Wilson intervals in the analysis field reproduce (water 111 of 116, 90.3-98.1; preloaded 32.8-50.5; postloaded 38.6-56.4), and the continuity-corrected frequency-postloading test gives p = 0.057 as stated.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract generalizes awareness of harm to people who use ecstasy, rounds 38.8% to 'forty percent', and the Discussion's 'unlikely to cause harm' and Dutch death-reduction statements rest on no data and a newspaper report (p. 174). One fix: 'only from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments' should read 'most with injected pre-treatments' (p. 174).

missed: The paper glosses the 'comedown' as the acute recovery period (p. 169, Introduction 2nd paragraph); the claim's 'in the days after' is the editors' gloss, not the paper's.

Table 6 (p. 173): 21.8% of the 55 who gave reasons pre- or postloaded to increase the pleasurable effects of ecstasy (the third most common reason, above reducing side effects, 18.2%); the card has it in key finding 7, but the claim's magnitude omits it, so the claim presents pre- and postloading as purely protective in intent. The authors also raise the concern that people may keep or increase their use believing they are protected (p. 174, Discussion 12th paragraph).

The paper treats SSRIs inconsistently: p. 174 cites rat studies in which fluoxetine pre-treatment protected against MDMA's effects, while p. 175 lists SSRIs with 5-HTP and St John's wort as substances that 'augment the release of serotonin' and risk serotonin syndrome (SSRIs block reuptake). Not a number error; the claim's serotonin-syndrome line should stay attributed to the authors as a caution, with no data from the sample.

Shares among the 46, 54 and 55 respondents who listed products or reasons carry 95% intervals of about +/-12 to +/-14 points (for example 5-HTP before 41.3% of 46, Wilson 28.3-55.7%), wider than the +/-9 points the card and claim give for whole-sample shares.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Not every chemical group is concentrated in the 1968-69 bin: the benzene panel peaks in 1967 (about 3) and has about 1 in 1968-69; trichloroethane had about 3 in 1964 and 2 in 1966, so 'isolated deaths' before 1967 means up to about 3 a year. The same wording in analysis.effect_sizes ('largest counts for every chemical group in the combined 1968-1969 bin') needs the same fix. Fluorocarbon 49 and toluene 6 in the last bin confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high for anything beyond description is right. METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series (the card states the round brief directed JBI; this reader did not open that brief). Domain 6 note: 'so most were attributed from circumstances' is an inference, as above.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract asserts a sharply rising incidence rate, a West Coast origin, a social preponderance and arrhythmia as the most likely explanation, none with denominators or recordings, while the Comment itself calls the cause of the terminal event difficult to say. The Comment's 'frequently' for exercise or stress before death rests on 18 of 110 listed.

missed: Benzene's yearly panel peaks in 1967, not in the last bin (see key finding 2).
The fluorocarbon yearly panel appears to total about 58 against 59 on the map (approximate reading).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist is the right instrument for an opinion piece (METHODS 5.3); overall 'high' is not less severe than the worst domain, and the three 'high' domains match what I read (no search, no appraisal of cited work, reliance on the group's own studies).

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: the only data are a methods-free figure, and the running text overstates that figure in three places.

missed: Figure 3's coefficients are on two different scales (predictors 0.16 to 0.46, experience-to-well-being 1.96 and -1.12), which suggests that not all of them are standardized; worth recording beside the card's note that the coefficient type is unreported, because the well-being paths cannot be read as standardized betas.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is right for a systematic review, and critically low follows from the unmet critical items (no protocol, restricted search, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal, risk of bias ignored in interpretation). Item 4 as 'no' is a defensible reading: the language restriction removed 1,282 records and is not justified.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it substantial rather than minor. The discussion concludes from five uncontrolled open-label reports that psychedelics have a therapeutic effect independent of context (p. 17), a causal reading the review's own design cannot support and that sits against its statement that no trial compared settings; the abstract also carries two figures that the Results contradict (763 participants, psilocybin 47%). The card documents all of this, so the difference is in the rating word only.

missed: Possible double counting in the pre-session paragraph (p. 8): Gasser et al. (2014) appears both among trials with one preparatory interview and among those with two, so the per-number lists do not add to the 19 trials stated in the same sentence.

The review contains no statement of who scored the 16 sub-domains or whether the scoring was duplicated, which the card records under exposure and AMSTAR item 6 but not as a reporting issue; it is the reason the Table 2 counts cannot be reproduced independently without re-reading all 27 articles.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Minor wording: the case with 137 mmol/L on day one and 129 on day three is one of the 36 rows with a sodium value (counted at its lowest, 129), not a further, 37th row; 36 with a value and 16 without make 52, as outcomes.operationalization says. The same parenthesis in analysis.effect_sizes needs the same change. All other counts confirmed (52 rows, 46 women, 6 men, ages 13-49, MDMA in 50, 21/27/3/1 outcomes, sodium 101-130, deaths 109-126).

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, follows the worst domains; consistent with what this reader found in Table 3.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. For gap (4), the specific count: the amount is unknown for 14 of the table's 21 deaths, and the review's single-dose statement is limited to deaths or permanent neurological injury in women aged 15 to 30 (p. 10).

missed: Table 3's first row (Salathe et al., 2018) lists the substance as methamphetamine, but the reference title (p. 14) is 'SIADH and water intoxication related to ecstasy'; its sodium and outcome are given as Unknown.
46 of 52 is 88.5%; the review prints 89% (p. 7).
The 10 Rosenson et al. (2007) fatal rows include 9 women, so the California series also contributes to the women's share.

key_findings_flagged.correction: 'digit span was unchanged' can be read as digit span not being impaired. The review says CBD pre-treatment did not seem to alter THC's impairing effects on working-memory tasks, including digit span forward and backward (3.6.6.2, p. 25). Suggested wording: 'and CBD did not change THC's impairment of working memory, including digit span'.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 without meta-analysis; critically low follows from items 4 and 13. Item 13 is a close call, as the card says, but the discussion draws its anxiety and psychosis conclusion as 'significantly fewer' from studies including two with some concerns while calling risk of bias typically low, so 'no' is defensible.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor overall because the abstract is hedged; the discussion's statement on anxiety and psychosis-like effects (p. 33) is the gap most likely to travel, and the card records it.

missed: Cannabis-use frequency: the card's 'mostly with occasional use' (cannot_establish) and 'most other samples had used occasionally' (sample demographics) are not established by Table 1: about half of Bird et al.'s 155 used at least weekly (p. 66), 24 of the 48 in the Hindocha/Morgan study used daily (p. 68), Haney et al.'s 31 were current users (p. 68), and Englund, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie and Karniol give only 'at least once' (pp. 67, 69). The claim's 'mostly occasionally' appears to come from here.
Men-only samples: counting Dalton's two experiments as Table 1 does, six studies enrolled men only (Dalton twice, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt, Karniol), not five.
Hunt et al.'s CBD timing differs between the text (8, 6 and 2 h before THC, p. 18) and Table 1 (480, 300 and 120 min, p. 69).
Arkell et al.: Table 1 says three of the 14 did not complete (p. 65), while the text uses n = 14 throughout.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Main point confirmed (the 'fold reductions' are odds ratios; amount not measured). Correction to the description: in a proportional-odds model the odds ratio is the common ratio for a lower category at both cut-points, not only 'less or none rather than the same or more'; with the Overall probabilities the two cuts give 4.20 and 4.32. The consequence stands: less or none 9.0% against 2.3%, more 6.3% against 22.5%, so most of the absolute contrast is fewer reports of using more.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious overall; no domain critical. Agree with each domain judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's fold reductions and 'assist PWUD to immediately reduce their risks', the Discussion's 'actual reduction in amount of drugs used' (p. 6) and the Conclusions' 'compelling evidence for the impact of FTS' and 'primarily reducing the amount of fentanyl used' (p. 8), against self-reported associations in which the same amount followed 85% of positive results. The 'primarily reducing the amount of fentanyl used' wording is also at odds with Table 4, where the contrasts are smallest for illicit opioids only (OR 2.18).

missed: Internal inconsistency in Table 4 (p. 8; editors' calculation): the benzodiazepine row's modelled probabilities (positive 0.032 / 0.701 / 0.266; negative 0.009 / 0.334 / 0.657) imply odds ratios of about 3.6 (less or none against same or more) and 5.3 (less, none or same against more), not the printed 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27). The other rows reproduce approximately: overall 4.20 / 4.32 (printed 4.37), opioids only 2.18 / 2.10 (2.18), stimulants only 10.35 / 8.46 (10.04), opioids and stimulants 3.94 / 3.73 (4.21), other 2.03 / 2.01 (2.11). By the probabilities, stimulants only, not benzodiazepines, shows the largest contrast. The abstract's '20-fold' figure and the Discussion's 'strongest for those testing benzodiazepines' (p. 6) rest on the printed ratio. Claims (cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services) should not say the contrast was largest for benzodiazepines without this caveat.

The study did collect overdose (past 30 days at baseline, a covariate in every model, pp. 2-3), and the companion paper (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025, cited p. 3) reports overdoses during follow-up; this paper analyses no harm or overdose outcome. The card's 'not analysed' is right; the claim's 'measures neither harm nor overdose' is not.
Behaviour was asked for up to two strip uses a day, recalled in the weekly survey (p. 2), so 'each result' in claims should read 'up to two tests a day'.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 fits a parallel-group randomized trial, and 'some concerns' overall matches the worst domains. The domains rest partly on what the letter omits rather than on what it did, which the card states; the supplements, if read, could lower several of them.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' fits: the results are reported plainly, and the stretch is the word 'improving' without any clinical outcome, which the card records.

missed: The flow diagram counts patients 'lost to 8-week follow-up' in both arms, so the trial followed patients beyond the 4-week infusion course; the letter reports nothing from that follow-up, which reinforces the card's point that all non-haemodynamic outcomes are deferred.
The title and discussion speak of the haemodynamic response, but only blood pressure is reported: no heart rate or other haemodynamic measure appears in the letter.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 fits a randomized crossover with an objective outcome. Some concerns overall is right: the randomization method is not described, there is no protocol, and the paired comparisons the Methods announce are not reported; carryover is implausible with at least 7 days between single small doses.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the central result (lower peak and AUC after food at this dose) is reported accurately; the gaps are the composition statement resting on a test with power about 0.2, the unmeasured mechanisms and the unquantified 1-2 h elimination statement, all of which the card records.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Content correct. The 121 (51.1%) and none-after-placebo sentences are in Results 3.5.2, 1st paragraph (begins p. 26; these sentences at the top of the right column on p. 27), not a 2nd paragraph; the 2nd paragraph is the one-sentence dose-response statement. The 237 is printed on p. 26 (first sentence of 3.5.2) and in the abstract (p. 22); Table 1 footnote 2 is on p. 26 as stated.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from items 4, 11 and 13, each defensibly not met. Item 15 'yes' is generous (funnel plots with 6 studies; the flagged study was not followed up by a sensitivity analysis), but the overall rating does not change.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the counts support the abstract's panic conclusion; the gaps are the abstract's choice of one of two incompatible pooled ratios and its unqualified statement that caffeine increases anxiety, which the discussion itself grades as less certain.

missed: Dose of Charney et al. (1985): Table 1 calls it caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg (p. 25), while the text converts 10 mg/kg into about 750 mg of caffeine at 75 kg (p. 25). The review does not say whether the dose is expressed as caffeine or as the citrate salt (about half caffeine by weight); if the salt, that study's caffeine dose would be near 375 mg, which would change the 400-750 mg range and the statement that no study tested less than 400 mg. Needs the primary paper.
Fig. 2 shows blinding of participants and personnel unclear in about a fifth of studies, while Results 3.2.1 says patients were blinded in all studies (p. 25).
The pooled anxiety analysis uses Tancer et al.'s 90-min STAI value (g 0.23 in Fig. 3), although Tancer reported a larger rise in panic disorder than in controls only at 150 min (p. 26).

key_findings_flagged.correction: Numbers confirmed (Table 2 and text). Locator: Results, 5th paragraph (AM p. 7; the first paragraph to start on that page), not the 3rd; Table 2 (AM p. 19) correct.
Content confirmed (12 of 30 cited withdrawal). Locator: Results, 5th paragraph (AM p. 7), not the 3rd.
Numbers confirmed (21 of 24, 87.5%; 2 harm-reduction behaviour; 2 sold). Locator: Results, 6th paragraph (AM p. 7), not the 4th; Table 2 (AM p. 19) correct.

Numbers confirmed against Table 2 (31, 57.4%; 26 of 48, 54.2%; 17 of 24, 70.8%). Locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starts AM p. 6, ends AM p. 7), not the 3rd (the 3rd is the strip-use paragraph of key finding 3). The text itself gives other denominators (57.1% 'of the 57', 'of the 49', 'of the 25').

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical overall (confounding critical: single arm, co-delivered counselling and card on the same behaviours, non-users changed as much). Domain judgments agree. Wilson intervals in the analysis field reproduce (57/68 73.3-90.7; 33/48 54.7-80.1; 30/48 48.4-74.8; 65/68 87.8-98.5).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'short-term effectiveness' (AM p. 8) and the abstract's conclusion rest on an uncontrolled pre-post comparison with mismatched recall windows; the primary outcome is absent from the abstract; the Discussion calls the non-significant overdose change 'six times lower'.

missed: The Results text calls the after-result question 'an open-ended survey question' (AM p. 7, 5th and 6th paragraphs), while the Methods and Table 2 describe a select-all-that-apply question (AM pp. 5, 19); the format affects how the 69% and 63% should be read.

Table 3's overdose row uses 68 as its denominator (6/68 = 8.8%, 1/68 = 1.5%) although the section footnote says 'among n = 59 who reported opioid use at follow-up', which fits the solitary-use and asking-someone rows; no McNemar statistic or p-value is given for overdose (AM pp. 21-22).

The follow-up is called one month throughout (abstract, AM p. 1; hypothesis, AM p. 3; Methods, AM p. 4; Table 2 title, AM p. 19; Fig. 2, AM p. 16) although the mean was 56 days; Table 2's 'Used FTS in past month' therefore may not cover the whole interval. Claims citing 'not one month, as the review says' should note that the paper itself says one month.

Table 3's needle-exchange row does not add up: total 29 (42.7%) to 22 (32.4%), but strata 17 (77.3%) + 2 (66.7%) = 19 at baseline and 13 + 1 = 14 at follow-up, percentages that fit denominators of 22 and 3 (AM p. 22). Alcohol frequency is labelled 'at least daily' in Table 3 but was dichotomized as at least weekly in the Methods (AM pp. 5, 21). Not relevant to the current claims.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 is the right instrument for a randomized, counterbalanced within-person comparison (METHODS 5.3); 'some concerns' overall matches the worst domains, and the card is right to put the abstinence and session-3 comparisons outside the judgment as non-randomized.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' fits: the abstract says 'tended to be higher', and the main stretch is putting the non-randomized abstinence comparison in the abstract, which the card records.

missed: Internal inconsistency not on the card: the Results describe abstinence as confirmed by 'exhaled carbon dioxide, urinary cotinine, and participant self-report' (p. 474), while the Methods specify exhaled carbon monoxide, 6 ppm or less, with urine cotinine under 200 ng/mL (p. 476). Carbon dioxide is plainly a slip, but it is the only place the Results name the verification method.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: Six trials, not five, had three or more arms (Table 1, p. 6): Andersson 2015 (5 arms), Leeman 2016 (4), Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018, Braitman 2022, Martens 2013 and Sugarman and Carey 2009 (3 each). The rest of the issue stands; re-pooling the plotted estimates suggests the adjunct subgroup is the four adjunct trials only (frequency -0.13 reproduces from Andersson, Larimer and Leeman; adding the boosters gives -0.11), so the three booster trials appear to have been left out of the role comparison or analysed separately (editors' reconstruction; supplements not read).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, low confidence (provisional): item 4 'no' (English, peer-reviewed limits not justified; no registries or grey literature) is the one critical flaw; item 7 no information without Appendix 2; items 11 and 13 close calls as the card says. Item 9: the lenient D3 judgment for Arazan is noted; it does not change the rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, borderline moderate: the abstract gives only the post-removal strategy-use estimate (the prespecified pooled 0.58, p = 0.152, is absent), calls problems significant in sensitivity analysis, and states greater effects for two subgroups without a between-subgroup test; all three are labelled, and the alcohol results are reported fairly. The results text also calls overall risk of bias low to moderate (p. 5) when 14 of 15 trials had some concerns or high risk.

missed: Only 11 of the 15 trials enter any pooled estimate: Braitman and Henson 2016, Dvorak 2015, Edwards 2020 and LaBrie 2015 appear in none of Figs. 3-6, and no reason is given. They include two of the four trials credited with mediation through PBS (Dvorak, LaBrie) and one of the three with reduced harms (Edwards). Claims should say 'pooled from 9, 6, 7 and 6 of 11 trials' rather than imply a 15-trial meta-analysis.

Subgroup membership (editors' re-pooling of the plotted estimates, approximate): over 3 months = Braitman 2018, Kenney, Larimer, Leeman, Martens for quantity (-0.12) and Braitman 2018, Larimer, Leeman, Martens for frequency (-0.13); adjunct = Andersson, Larimer, Leeman, Neighbors. Larimer et al. (2007; mailed feedback with normative content, 12 months, the most precise trial) is in both 'larger effect' subgroups, so the two findings largely overlap.

The Methods describe influence diagnostics 'with sensitivity analyses conducted by excluding influential studies' (p. 3, 2.7). The card's 'not described as prespecified' is accurate (the word is used only for the subgroups), but the step was described as part of the analysis plan; the claim's 'a step not described as planned' goes beyond the paper.
The Discussion (p. 8, 2nd paragraph) cites Braitman 2022 as reducing alcohol outcomes without PBS change, but Table 3 marks Braitman 2022 'Alcohol reduction: No' (drinking declined in all arms).

Table 3's trial-level verdicts do not always match the pooled inputs: Kenney 2014 harm reduction 'Yes' against g -0.03 (-0.30 to 0.23) in Fig. 5; Neighbors 2009 PBS change 'Yes' against g 0.19 (-0.05 to 0.42) in Fig. 6; presumably other time points or measures, not explained.

The only low-risk trial (Martens 2013) found no effect on quantity (-0.12, -0.37 to 0.13), frequency (0.06) or problems (-0.15, -0.40 to 0.11) despite raising PBS use (0.49, 0.23 to 0.74) (Figs. 3-6).

The card's 'self-reported drinking and problems in every trial' (exposure) goes slightly beyond the paper, which lists reliance on self-reported outcomes as a limitation (p. 11) without saying every trial; Table 3 lists BAC outcomes (Andersson, Braitman and Henson, Neighbors) whose method is not described.
